name: Hüsker Dü
label: SST
lede: Bob Mould, Grant Hart and Greg Norton started in St. Paul in 1979, outran every band in the Midwest, then wrote a double album that gave hardcore a plot and a tune. Nine years in, they were done.

hero.by: Photo: Warner Bros. Records publicity photo, 1986

eras.title: Umlauts and a board game's name
eras.text: A Macalester freshman, a record-store clerk and the guy who beat that clerk to a job formed a band in St. Paul. They took the name of a board game, added umlauts, and landed at Jay's Longhorn Bar, the center of Minneapolis punk.

years.h: Grant Hart asks Bob Mould if he smokes pot, then suggests a band
years.p: Mould, a Macalester College freshman, kept coming into Cheapo Records in St. Paul, where Hart clerked, and they bonded over the [[Ramones|d6ed7887-a401-47a8-893c-34b967444d26]]. The band pitch came after a walk to Mould's dorm.
years.xp:
Mould's account in The Quietus: Hart told him "I'm a musician. I play drums," and when Mould said he played guitar, Hart answered, "No you don't. Do you smoke pot?" They smoked downstairs, walked to Mould's dorm a block or two away, and Mould played. Hart's verdict: "My name's Grant, we should start a band."

Hart already knew [[Greg Norton|c8e2b334-0b40-4c13-8970-92c86e6369b8]]: the two had applied for the same job, and Norton got it. Mould and Hart finally hung out at a Ramones concert that also featured Foreigner.

years.h: Mangling Psycho Killer gives the band its name
years.p: With keyboardist Charlie Pine, the trio starts out on covers. Fumbling the French words of the Talking Heads song Psycho Killer, they shout the name of a 1950s board game, Hūsker Dū?
years.xp:
Hūsker Dū? means do you remember? in Danish and Norwegian. The band added heavy metal umlauts to set themselves apart from the other hardcore bands.

From the summer of 1979 they practiced in the basement of Northern Lights, the record store where Norton worked.

years.h: The first gig is at Ron's Randolph Inn in St. Paul
years.p: The setlist is mostly covers and punk songs, played in a bar near the Macalester College campus.
years.xp: Forty years later to the day, on March 30, 2019, Bob Mould marked the anniversary in St. Paul on a bill with Norton's band Porcupine.

years.h: Charlie Pine gets fired in the middle of the third show
years.p: The keyboard goes with him. The band carries on as the trio of Mould, Hart and Norton.

years.h: Jay's Longhorn Bar gives the trio its first real gigs
years.p: The Longhorn is the center of the Minneapolis punk scene, and the place where Mould had first seen the [[Suicide Commandos|eb7988a4-4a66-4320-a6ea-d17da0da88ac]] up close.

eras.title: Faster than anyone on the bill
eras.text: The band started its own label, toured, and made records as fast as it played. SST wanted them but couldn't afford them yet, so Mike Watt's New Alliance Records stepped in, and by 1983 they were on SST for good.

years.h: The first record comes out on a label they started themselves
years.p: The debut 7-inch pairs Statues with Amusement and appears in January 1981 on Reflex Records.

years.h: "The Children's Crusade" is what they call the first tour
years.p: Summer 1981, on the road. Mould later described himself swinging a hammer and breaking bottles.
years.xp:
Norton remembered finding like-minded kids in every town: "We looked at it as this congruent revolution; it was cool to find like-minded people."

Mould said the band came home changed: "We picked up speed and anger across those few months. When we got back to Minneapolis, I don't think people recognised us."

years.h: Land Speed Record is one night at Duffy's, on tape
years.p: Hüsker Dü record a whole set live at Duffy's in Minneapolis. SST can't afford to put it out, so [[Mike Watt|568203ae-c27b-4990-8997-09c0d5c0de77]]'s New Alliance Records releases it in January 1982.
years.xp: Seventeen songs in 26 minutes. Norton told The Quietus: "When we started, we wanted to play faster than the Ramones." He remembered the Duffy's set as the last show of that summer's tour.

years.h: In a Free Land follows on New Alliance
years.p: Their second release on the label is a three-song single with the title track up front.

years.h: A Donovan cover sits in the middle of Everything Falls Apart
years.p: Their first studio album, a short hardcore blast, comes out on Reflex in January 1983. The cover is Donovan's Sunshine Superman.

yt: Diane, live at the 7th Street Entry, Sept. 5, 1981
years.h: Metal Circus is the first record on SST
years.p: A seven-song EP. Grant Hart's Diane is written about Diane Edwards, a West St. Paul waitress abducted and murdered in 1980.
years.xp: Hart sings Diane from the killer's point of view, and it became one of the band's most covered songs. The record showed both writers pulling away from pure speed.

eras.title: Three albums in fourteen months
eras.text: Between July 1984 and September 1985 they put out Zen Arcade, New Day Rising and Flip Your Wig, and critics began treating a St. Paul hardcore band as something bigger than hardcore. SST couldn't keep the records in the shops, and Warner Bros. came calling.

years.h: Hüsker Dü turn the Byrds' Eight Miles High into a roar
years.p: A non-album single on SST, cut in first takes like everything else. Mould called it the band's calling card, arriving right before Zen Arcade.

q: I think we've got a rock opera here!
Greg Norton, on assembling the songs
years.h: Zen Arcade runs a runaway boy through an entire double album
years.p: He escapes an abusive home into the army, religion, love and drugs, then wakes to find it was a dream. SST presses 3,500 to 5,000 copies, and they sell out.
years.xp:
Recorded in October 1983 at Total Access in Redondo Beach with producer [[Spot|d95a08a1-80f5-4232-bdb7-4777c369f0f9]]: 25 songs in 40 hours, all but Something I Learned Today and Newest Industry first takes, $3,200 all in. Mould called it "a 40-hour blur." Rolling Stone's David Fricke called it a kind of thrash Quadrophenia.

The album sat out of stock for months while the band toured, which infuriated them; it had sold 20,000 copies by spring 1985. Norton said SST greatly underestimated how many copies to press. SST released the [[Minutemen|d4ad0149-d8ae-4105-8009-0221fce9ff35]]'s Double Nickels on the Dime the same month.

years.h: Boston promoter David Savoy, 22, starts working with the band
years.p: Savoy had promoted two Hüsker Dü shows in Massachusetts, one in Concord that December. He's soon their manager.
years.xp: Mould on why he fit: "He was tied into the Boston-area music scene, and he knew a lot of the same people we did."

yt: Full set at the Camden Palace, London, 1985
years.h: New Day Rising hides pop songs under a wall of noise
years.p: Out six months after Zen Arcade, with Celebrated Summer and I Apologize. It lands in the Village Voice Pazz & Jop top ten.

years.h: A hometown night at First Avenue, 23 songs deep
years.p: The show is two weeks before New Day Rising comes out. The tape survived the 2011 fire at Grant Hart's house and was released in 2025 as 1985: The Miracle Year.

years.h: Warner Bros. calls while they're cutting Flip Your Wig
years.p: Warner promises total creative control. Mould also points at SST's distribution: some in-store signings had no records to sign.
years.xp:
Norton called Warner "the most artist-friendly label out there," and said the label promised to let Hüsker Dü be Hüsker Dü.

Mould was less settled: "I felt bad about abandoning the independent music scene we'd helped to create." His case against SST: "We had the momentum, and they were hanging us out to dry."

years.cap: Bob Mould, Grant Hart and Greg Norton in a record store, March 1985
yt: Makes No Sense at All, live, 1985
years.h: Flip Your Wig is the first indie album to top the CMJ chart
years.p: Self-produced and released on SST nine months after New Day Rising, with Makes No Sense at All and Green Eyes. It's their last indie record.

eras.title: A Warner deal and a band coming apart
eras.text: On paper the Warner years worked: network TV, a double album, a real manager. Underneath, Mould had quit drinking, Hart was using heroin, the two were fighting over how many songs each got, and the manager who'd joined them was dead by February 1987.

years.h: Candy Apple Grey brings Hüsker Dü to Warner Bros.
years.p: The major-label debut reaches No. 140 on the Billboard 200, with Hart's Don't Want to Know If You Are Lonely and Mould's acoustic Hardly Getting Over It.
play: Don't Want to Know If You Are Lonely

years.h: The two songwriters head in opposite directions in 1986
years.p: Mould quits drinking. Hart's heroin addiction takes hold after the Candy Apple Grey tour.

years.h: Hart says Mould capped his songs at 45 percent of any record
years.p: Warehouse: Songs and Stories, cut at Nicollet Studios in Minneapolis, is a 20-song double album: eleven Mould songs, nine Hart. It peaks at No. 117.
years.xp: Mould had insisted on separate songwriting credits since Zen Arcade. By Warehouse the tally between the two writers had become a war.

years.h: Manager David Savoy dies by suicide at 24
years.p: Mould on Savoy's death in February 1987, on the eve of the Warehouse tour.
years.xp:
Mould said everyone "retreated into their own corners and dealt with that in their own particular ways."

In 2006 Hart told Q magazine he took full responsibility, saying working for both him and Mould had forced Savoy into a two-faced situation: "I take full responsibility for [Savoy's] suicide."

yt: Today Show, May 20, 1987: interview and Could You Be the One?
years.h: Joan Rivers and the Today show get a Hüsker Dü set each
years.p: On April 27, 1987 they play Could You Be the One? and She's a Woman (And Now He Is a Man) on Fox's Late Show Starring Joan Rivers. NBC's Today has them in the studio on May 20.

years.src: Wikipedia: Hüsker Dü · The Quietus · Internet Archive
years.h: The last show happens in Columbia, Missouri, with Hart in withdrawal
years.p: Mould's description in his memoir. Hart was on methadone to quit heroin, but his bottle had leaked. Mould cancels the rest of the tour.
years.xp:
The show was at the Blue Note. Hart insisted he could keep going; Mould and Norton didn't believe it.

Mould has given three reasons for the split: Hart's drug use and new relationship, Norton's new marriage and businesses, and his own sobriety. Looking back in 2020, he called that night "the period at the end of an 18-month run-on sentence."

years.h: Mould quits at a band meeting, and Hüsker Dü is done
years.p: The meeting is on January 26; by the 28th the band is over.
years.xp: Mould, in The Quietus: "Things reached a point where I was just, 'This is enough'. It had to end."

eras.title: Separate corners
eras.text: Mould and Hart went solo within a year and spent the 1990s in separate bands, Sugar and Nova Mob. Norton left music to cook. Until 2004 the two songwriters never shared a stage.

years.h: Mould's Workbook and Hart's Intolerance land the same year
years.p: Workbook is on Virgin, Intolerance on SST. Late in 1989 Hart starts [[Nova Mob|06b7e37f-444b-43b2-97eb-1e92efdb6512]], named for William Burroughs' Nova Express; in 1992 Mould forms [[Sugar|e3347fbd-2595-480e-926d-278566debf9d]]. Both new bands are gone by the mid-1990s.

years.h: The Living End puts the last tour on record
years.p: A live album from the October 1987 Warehouse tour, issued by Warner Bros. Mould says he has never listened to it.

years.h: For the first time since 1987, Mould and Hart play together
years.p: At a Minneapolis benefit for [[Soul Asylum|b10db9ad-b4c3-47f3-a7a4-37864b134f65]] bassist Karl Mueller, then being treated for cancer, Mould brings Hart out for Never Talking to You Again and Hardly Getting Over It.
years.xp: Mould warned it shouldn't raise false hope of a reunion. Norton, meanwhile, was running a restaurant, The Nortons, in Red Wing, Minnesota.

eras.title: The tapes that survived
eras.text: Hart's 2006 Magnet interview ended reunion talk, but the three eventually agreed on how to handle the catalog. Hart died in 2017, months after he and Mould cleared things up, and the Numero Group has been opening the vaults since.

years.cap: Bob Mould live in Dublin, February 2, 2006
years.h: Hart tells Magnet what he thinks of Mould, and reunion talk ends
years.p: In the 2006 interview Hart harshly criticizes Mould, effectively ending any prospect of a Hüsker Dü reunion. Norton returns to music with Gang Font.

years.src: Wikipedia: Hüsker Dü · The Second Disc
years.h: Grant Hart's house burns down, taking part of the archive
years.p: The January 1985 First Avenue tapes are among what survives.

years.h: The band opens an official website and a merch store
years.p: Norton tells the Star Tribune that he, Mould and Hart have worked out a licensing agreement.

years.h: Grant Hart dies of liver cancer at 56
years.p: He dies at Fairview University of Minnesota hospital from liver cancer and complications of hepatitis C. Mould's statement praises him as a visual artist, storyteller and musician.
years.xp: Mould said the two had met earlier that year and cleared everything up, laughing about the past and crying a little. Hart had married Brigid McGough on July 5, 2017.

years.h: The Numero Group opens the vault with Savage Young Dü
years.p: Three CDs or four LPs of demos, studio tracks and live recordings from the first four years, out two months after Hart's death.

years.h: On the 40th anniversary, Mould and Norton share a bill
years.p: In St. Paul on March 30, 2019, Mould plays on a bill with Norton's band Porcupine and sings Hart's Never Talking to You Again.

years.h: 1985: The Miracle Year brings out the lost First Avenue tape
years.p: Numero Group releases the January 30, 1985 show plus 20 more live tracks from that year, recorded in the U.S. and Europe.
years.xp: The set runs 43 tracks across two CDs or four LPs, with 36 pages of liner notes. The second disc pulls from stops including Salt Lake City, Boulder, Long Beach, Washington, Hoboken, Frankfurt and Lausanne.
